name: The Rockwood Oak

location.address: Western shore of Wirth Lake, Theodore Wirth Regional Park, 1 Theodore Wirth Pkwy

access: Free. Stands in a public regional park, embedded in thick woods on the park's southern end near the lake; a trail runs past it but the tree itself takes some looking to spot.
transport: Theodore Wirth Regional Park, northwest Minneapolis; reachable by Metro Transit bus, no rail stop directly at the park.
story:
The tornado that tore through north Minneapolis in 2011 hit this bur oak and did not finish it. It is still standing, and it may well be the oldest living thing in the city. The Minneapolis Parks Foundation puts it at 315 years; Mpls.St.Paul Magazine says approximately 300. Both of them call it a candidate for the city's oldest tree, which is a claim nobody has been able to settle.

Bur oak is the species that makes that plausible. It is the oak of the prairie edge, with bark thick enough to survive the fires that used to run through the oak savanna every few years, which is why Minnesota's true veterans are bur oaks rather than something more delicate. This one carries burls, the lumpy carbuncle-like growths that show on a trunk with a long history behind it.

It had been growing for a century before Fort Snelling went up at the river junction downstream, and the city came later still. It is named for C.J. Rockwood, who helped expand the park around it; Theodore Wirth Regional Park grew up around the tree rather than the other way round.

Finding it takes patience. It sits in thick woods on the western shore of Wirth Lake, near the southern end of the park, and the trail goes past without announcing it. Nobody has published a girth figure, which is an odd gap for a tree with this claim on it.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the burls on the trunk, the lumpy growths that mark its age, on a bur oak. It stands in thick woods on the western shore of Wirth Lake, near the southern end of Theodore Wirth Park, just off the trail.
why_go: A roughly 300-year-old bur oak, one of the likely oldest living things in Minneapolis, that took a direct hit from the 2011 tornado and is still standing, its trunk marked with age burls.

name: The Shoe Tree

location.address: Bohemian Flats Park, Mississippi Gorge Regional Park, west bank of the Mississippi near the Washington Avenue Bridge

access: Free. Public riverside park beside the Washington Avenue Bridge on the University of Minnesota's West Bank.
transport: University of Minnesota West Bank campus; served by campus and city bus routes and the West Bank light rail station, short walk down to Bohemian Flats.
story:
Nobody agrees on why the shoes go up. University of Minnesota students have been throwing tied-together pairs into the branches of this hackberry since at least 1995, when the Minnesota Daily first wrote about it, and the explanations on offer run from graduation ritual to end-of-exams release to no reason anyone can name. The shoes hang until weather or the park takes them down. More arrive.

It is a common hackberry, and that is the honest description: a plain North American tree with rough corky bark and no claim at all to age or size. Nobody has dated it and nobody has measured it. It is here because it is a landmark, which it unarguably is, with its own Wikipedia page and a University of Minnesota Libraries piece written about it, which is more attention than almost any other tree in this city gets.

It stands in Bohemian Flats Park on the west bank of the Mississippi, directly under the Washington Avenue Bridge, on ground where an immigrant settlement of Bohemian, Slovak and Scandinavian families lived down in the river flats until the city cleared them out. The park kept their name.

Go near the end of a semester if you want to catch the tradition in motion. The rest of the year it is a hackberry wearing what other people left behind.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the shoes, pairs tied together and thrown up into the branches for thirty years. It stands in Bohemian Flats Park on the west bank of the Mississippi, directly under the Washington Avenue Bridge.
why_go: A hackberry beside the Washington Avenue Bridge that University of Minnesota students have been hanging tied-together shoes from since at least the 1990s, for reasons nobody agrees on; it has its own Wikipedia page and is one of the campus's odder rituals.

name: The Windom Park Basswood

location.address: Windom Park, 2251 NE Hayes St, southwest of the park building

transport: Northeast Minneapolis, Windom Park neighbourhood; served by city bus routes.
story:
The largest American basswood recorded in Minnesota is standing in an ordinary neighbourhood park in Northeast Minneapolis, hanging out over a slope behind the park building, with nothing there to tell you so. The Minneapolis Parks Foundation and Mpls.St.Paul Magazine both name it the state champion of its species, and both note the Park Board's Heritage Tree designation. Neither prints a height or a circumference, which is a strange gap for a tree whose entire claim is size.

Basswood is the American lime, and for a fortnight around the turn of June into July it does something an oak never will. The flowers are small, pale and hanging, the scent carries the width of a park, and bees work a tree this size hard enough that you hear it before you reach it. Beekeepers here set their year by the basswood flow.

The rest of the year it is a broad, heart-leaved shade tree, which is what basswoods were planted for along American streets by the thousand.

Nobody has dated it, and champion status is about size rather than years: basswood grows quickly, so a big one need not be an old one. You will find it southwest of the park building on NE Hayes Street, leaning out over the hillside. If anyone has the measurements, we would like them.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, the largest American basswood recorded in Minnesota, and by heart-shaped leaves on a tree leaning out over a slope. It stands just southwest of the park building in Windom Park, off NE Hayes Street.

best_time.label: late June into early July, when the basswood flowers and the whole crown hums with bees

why_go: Minnesota's state champion American basswood, the largest of its kind recorded in the state, growing over a hillside in an ordinary Northeast Minneapolis neighbourhood park.
